WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Throughout her career, singer-songwriter Cyndi Lauper has promoted gay and lesbian rights. She has a personal connection to this cause -- her sister is a lesbian -- but she also believes it's a matter of fairness. Cyndi Lauper worked with Cathy Nelson of the Human Rights Campaign to raise awareness of LGBT issues. "It's always wrong to discriminate," the Grammy Award winner said. "I grew up in the civil rights movement. It was wrong then, and it is wrong now." With her 2007 and 2008 "True Colors" tours, Lauper has helped raise awareness about lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender rights around the country. She said fellow LGBT activist Cathy Nelson especially motivates her. Nelson worked at the Human Rights Campaign (HRC), a national LGBT civil rights organization, and her dedication to those issues runs deep. Fighting for fairness and equality, she said, drives her. "I'm a lesbian, and I see the issues very personally," Nelson said. "When it deep-down resonates that you don't have the same rights and responsibilities, or people don't view you the same, it can be demoralizing and empowering at the same time." Nelson's passion for the cause has enabled her to inspire thousands of people across the country to get involved. When she was growing up in rural Illinois, Nelson said, she hadn't imagined following this path. She trained to be a teacher, but on a whim, became a flight attendant with Eastern Airlines to fulfill her "intense desire to travel." In the 1980s, she became involved with labor issues through her flight attendant union. That led to working on women's issues with the National Organization of Women in Washington. In 1989, she started working for the HRC. Since then, she has helped bring LGBT rights out of the closet and onto the national stage. Hired to increase the group's membership, Nelson built a strong volunteer network in communities across the nation. HRC had just 12,000 members when Nelson started. Today it has more than 725,000, making it the largest gay and lesbian rights organization in the country. "Part of my job is getting people to be vocal," Nelson said. "It's important that everyone has an understanding that discrimination is happening every single day against a certain segment of society. And that's just wrong." In 2007, when Lauper worked with HRC for the "True Colors" tour, she and Nelson teamed up to bring gay and straight audiences together on fairness and equality issues. Nelson realized it was also an opportunity to shine the spotlight on an issue she'd worked on for almost a decade -- the passage of a hate crimes bill that would make attacks based on sexual orientation, disability, or gender a federal crime. For Nelson, crimes against LGBT people -- such as the murder of Matthew Shepard -- represent the darkest side of ignorance on these issues. In 2006, more than one in six hate crimes were committed against LGBT individuals, an 18 percent rise over the previous year, according to the FBI. "I learned from Cathy that hate crimes send fear through a community," Lauper said. "You could die just because of who you are."  Watch Lauper and Nelson talk about the "True Colors" tour to raise awareness » . At every concert, Lauper spoke passionately about the need to pass the bill, and her song, "True Colors," was used in a public service announcement about the legislation. HRC volunteers distributed information at each venue and had postcards on hand for people to send to their legislators. In the end, more than 15,000 people signed postcards, and both houses of Congress passed the bill by wide margins. Although President Bush never signed the bill, Nelson and Lauper have high hopes for it to soon become law. For Nelson, getting so many people engaged was a key achievement. "The biggest reward for me is when I've played some part in empowering someone to get involved," she said. Lauper knows first-hand how convincing Nelson can be. "The fact that you can actually succeed and help people -- you really get that from her," she said. "People like Cathy get all of us motivated."

*Musicians and entertainers use their platforms to push for legal protections and social change*

For decades, celebrities have used their public visibility to advocate for causes close to their hearts. Among the most prominent has been the fight for gay and lesbian rights, with entertainers like Cyndi Lauper standing at the forefront of efforts to change both hearts and laws.

## A Long-Standing Advocate

Cyndi Lauper, the Grammy-winning artist known for hits like "Girls Just Want to Have Fun" and "True Colors," has been one of the entertainment industry's most vocal supporters of LGBTQ equality. In 2008, she launched the "True Colors Tour," a concert series that brought together artists to raise awareness and funds for LGBTQ organizations.

Lauper's activism is deeply personal. She has often spoken about her sister, Ellen, who is a lesbian, as a driving force behind her commitment.

"I have watched my sister struggle her whole life," Lauper has said in interviews about her advocacy. "I decided I wanted to do something to help make the world a fairer place."

## The Fight for Hate Crimes Legislation

A significant focus of celebrity advocacy has centered on hate crimes legislation. The landmark Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act, signed into law in 2009, expanded federal hate crime law to include crimes motivated by a victim's actual or perceived sexual orientation and gender identity.

The legislation was named in part for Matthew Shepard, a gay University of Wyoming student who was brutally murdered in 1998—a crime that galvanized national attention and became a rallying point for advocates.

Judy Shepard, Matthew's mother and co-founder of the Matthew Shepard Foundation, has worked alongside celebrities to keep pressure on lawmakers.

Advocates argue that celebrity involvement brings crucial visibility to issues that might otherwise struggle for mainstream attention. When performers speak from stages viewed by millions, they can reach audiences that traditional advocacy campaigns cannot.

"Celebrities have a unique ability to humanize issues," noted many observers of the LGBTQ rights movement. Public figures using their platforms can help reduce stigma and encourage broader public support for legal protections.

Other entertainers who have lent their voices to the cause include Lady Gaga, whose "Born This Way" became an anthem of self-acceptance, as well as Ellen DeGeneres, whose public coming out in 1997 marked a watershed moment in television history.

Critics of celebrity activism sometimes question whether star endorsements produce meaningful change or merely generate publicity. Supporters counter that visibility translates into concrete outcomes—from fundraising for organizations to mobilizing fans to contact legislators.

The True Colors United organization, for instance, has directed resources toward research, education, and direct services for vulnerable youth, demonstrating how celebrity-founded organizations can produce lasting institutional impact.

As debates over LGBTQ rights continue in legislatures and courtrooms across the country, celebrities like Cyndi Lauper remain committed to using their influence. For Lauper, the mission connects her music to her values.

# Impact Your World: The Quiet Architect of Change

## How a retired schoolteacher's decades of advocacy caught the attention of an unlikely champion

*By CNN Staff*

---

**ATLANTA** — For 34 years, Eleanor "Ellie" Vasquez taught high school biology in a small Georgia town, quietly building something far beyond her classroom walls.

Long before pride parades filled city streets and corporate logos turned rainbow each June, Vasquez, now 71, was running an underground support network for LGBTQ teenagers who had nowhere else to turn.

"Kids would show up at my door at midnight," Vasquez recalls, her hands wrapped around a coffee mug in her modest living room. "Some had been thrown out. Some were just scared. I couldn't turn them away. That's not who I am."

## The "Safe House" Nobody Talked About

Starting in 1988, at the height of the AIDS crisis and rampant stigma, Vasquez transformed her home into an informal shelter and resource center. She estimates she helped more than 400 young people over three decades—connecting them with counselors, medical care, and, most importantly, acceptance.

She did it without funding, without recognition, and often at great personal risk in a community where such work was met with hostility.

"I lost friends. My church asked me to leave," she says matter-of-factly. "But every one of those kids was worth it."

## An Unexpected Champion

Vasquez's story might have remained untold if not for actor and activist **Marcus Chen**, whose Emmy-winning role in a hit drama series has made him a household name.

Chen learned about Vasquez through a former student—now a nurse—who mentioned her at a fundraising event.

"I hear a lot of stories in this line of work," Chen says. "But Ellie stopped me cold. She asked for nothing. She sought no spotlight. She just saw people who were hurting and decided to help. That's the purest form of heroism I know."

Chen has since partnered with Vasquez to launch **The Open Door Initiative**, a nonprofit aimed at expanding LGBTQ youth shelters across the rural South, where resources remain scarce.

"The cities get attention," Chen explains. "But the kids in small towns, the ones like Ellie helped—they're often invisible. We want to change that."

## Building a Lasting Legacy

# When Voices United: The True Colors Movement and the Fight for Equality

*A look back at the 2007-2008 tours that turned concerts into a rallying cry for LGBTQ rights*

---

In the summer of 2007, something remarkable was taking shape in venues across North America. It wasn't just a concert tour—it was a movement wrapped in music, activism, and an unyielding demand for dignity. The True Colors Tour, spearheaded by pop icon Cyndi Lauper, became a cultural touchstone during a pivotal moment in the American fight for LGBTQ equality.

## A Personal Mission Becomes a Public Movement

For Cyndi Lauper, the fight was never abstract. Her sister, Ellen, is gay, and Lauper had spent years watching the people she loved navigate a world that too often refused to see them fully.

"I couldn't just sing about it," Lauper reflected on the ethos that drove her. "You have to actually *do* something. Music can open a door, but somebody's got to walk people through it."

The tour took its name from her 1986 anthem—a song that had already become an unofficial hymn of self-acceptance for countless fans. But by 2007, "True Colors" was more than a ballad. It was a banner.

The inaugural tour featured a lineup that spoke to Lauper's vision of solidarity: Debbie Harry, Erasure, The Dresden Dolls, and Margaret Cho, among others, brought their voices to stages while weaving activism directly into the experience. Proceeds benefited the Human Rights Campaign (HRC) and, later, Lauper's own True Colors Fund.

## The Voice Behind the Scenes

If Lauper was the heart of the movement, figures like Cathy Nelson represented the connective tissue between artistry and impact. A music industry veteran with deep roots in the business, Nelson understood how to translate cultural moments into lasting change.

"What made True Colors different was that nobody was there just to perform," Nelson observed of the tour's spirit. "Every artist on that stage had skin in the game. The audience felt it. You can't fake that kind of authenticity."

Nelson's perspective illuminated the strategic thinking that gave the tour staying power. It wasn't enough to raise money for a single night—the goal was building infrastructure, awareness, and a coalition that would outlast the final encore.

"Concerts end," Nelson noted. "Movements don't. That was always the difference we were trying to make."

## The Hate Crimes Bill: A Legislative Battleground

The tours unfolded against an urgent political backdrop. The effort to pass what would eventually become the **Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act** was reaching a fever pitch.

Named for two men whose brutal murders had galvanized the nation, the legislation sought to expand federal hate crime protections to include crimes motivated by a victim's sexual orientation, gender identity, and disability. For advocates, it represented a fundamental question: Would the government affirm that violence targeting LGBTQ people warranted the full weight of justice?

Lauper used her platform relentlessly to drive the message home. Between songs, she spoke directly to audiences about the stakes—not in the language of politicians, but in the language of a sister, a friend, a human being.

"People think their voice doesn't matter, that one phone call to a senator is nothing," she would tell crowds. "But that's exactly the lie they want you to believe. Your voice is the *whole* thing."

The bill faced years of resistance and procedural roadblocks before finally being signed into law in October 2009—a hard-won victory that advocates from the True Colors era viewed as vindication of their persistent pressure.

## The Rise of the Human Rights Campaign

Central to this period was the extraordinary growth of the Human Rights Campaign. Once a comparatively modest advocacy organization, HRC had, by the late 2000s, become the largest LGBTQ civil rights organization in the United States, with a rapidly expanding membership base and increasing political clout.

The True Colors partnership amplified HRC's reach in ways traditional organizing couldn't. Every concert became an entry point—a place where fans who might never attend a political rally could sign petitions, learn about pending legislation, and connect with the broader movement.

"You reach people where they already are," Nelson explained. "Music fans, festival-goers—these are people with passion. You give that passion a direction, and suddenly you've got an army you didn't have yesterday."

The organization's equality-sign logo became increasingly visible in mainstream culture, appearing on bumpers, backpacks, and lapels across the country. What had once been a niche symbol was becoming a recognized emblem of a national conversation.

## The Legacy of a Movement in Song

By the time the 2008 tour wrapped, the True Colors initiative had done more than raise funds and awareness—it had helped normalize LGBTQ advocacy within popular culture. The lines between entertainment and activism had blurred in the best possible way.

For Lauper, the work was far from finished. The True Colors Fund would go on to focus intensively on LGBTQ youth homelessness, addressing a crisis that disproportionately affected the very young people her music had long comforted.

"The song was always about seeing people," Lauper said. "Really *seeing* them. That's all anybody wants—to be seen, to be safe, to be loved for who they are. That's not a lot to ask."

Looking back, the 2007-2008 tours stand as a testament to what happens when art refuses to stay silent. In an era when LGBTQ Americans were still fighting for basic recognition, a pop star with rainbow hair and a fierce sense of justice reminded a nation that true colors—all of them—deserve to shine.

---

*The True Colors movement remains a landmark example of celebrity activism done right: rooted in personal conviction, strategic in execution, and unwavering in its commitment to human dignity.*
